title: His mother stood (John 19:25–27)
hookLine: Mary at the foot of the cross, given to the beloved disciple as his mother

cards: A hospital corridor at three in the morning. Nothing to do. Nothing to fix.
People stay because leaving is unthinkable. Now, the hill. Mark says that at the arrest his disciples all left him and fled.
But John's Gospel slows down and names who is standing by the cross: his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalen.
And one disciple, never named, whom the Gospel calls the disciple whom Jesus loved. They can't stop it. They can't change any of it.

teach.b: Jesus spends some of his last words on this. In the Douay-Rheims: "Woman, behold thy son." And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother."
John adds: "And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own." Woman can sound cold in English.
In John it's the same word he used for her at the wedding at Cana, a word of respect, and some readers hear an echo of the first woman in Genesis. Catholics hear this moment two ways, and hold both.

teach.h: A SON MAKES SURE HIS MOTHER HAS A HOME.
teach.b: The first is simple and human: a dying son makes sure his mother will have a home. The second is bigger.
The Gospel never names the beloved disciple. Tradition says it was John. Some readers say leaving him unnamed lets every disciple stand in his place.

So Catholics read it as Jesus giving his mother to all of us, and they call Mary the Mother of the Church, a title Pope Paul VI gave her during the Second Vatican Council. Then there's the word stood.
In the Latin Bible the verse opens with stabant, they stood, all of them together.
A medieval hymn takes the word for her alone: Stabat Mater, the mother stood.
It belongs to the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows, and parishes sing it at the Stations of the Cross. She didn't faint. She didn't leave.

how: Catholics sing or pray the Stabat Mater during the Stations of the Cross, especially in Lent, and honor Mary as Mother of the Church on the Monday after Pentecost.

games.q: you're dying, and your mother is standing below you. you have only a few words left. what do you do with them?
o: give her to your friend, and your friend to her.
games.why: "woman, behold thy son... behold thy mother." he spends his breath making sure she has a home, and Catholics hear him giving her to everyone.

practice: Bring to mind someone who mothered you, by birth or not: a mother, a grandmother, an aunt, a teacher, a neighbor, and see their face.
Then bring to mind someone who may have no one looking after them, an older woman on your street, a mother raising children alone, and choose one practical thing for them: a meal, a ride, an hour.
If you pray, you can ask Mary to look after them too.

wordCard.voice: Stabat Mater. Latin for the mother stood, a hymn for Mary keeping watch at the foot of the cross.

orig.note: Latin: the mother stood. the opening of a medieval hymn. the Latin Gospel itself has stabant, they stood.

carryVoice: Your line: behold thy mother. From that hour, she had a home. Day sixty-five, done.
